_comment: Cram-specific interview vocabulary. Loaded by the 🅰 Glossary modal on cram paths. Distinct from data/mechanics.json (code-idiom tags); these are interview-prep concepts.

terms.def: Always moving in one direction — non-decreasing or non-increasing. A monotonic stack only keeps elements in sorted order; popping smaller-than-current ones.
terms.where: Daily Temperatures, Sliding Window Maximum, Largest Rectangle in Histogram.

terms.def: When you iterate a structure, you get items back in the order you inserted them. Map and Set guarantee this; plain Object historically did not.
terms.where: "I need to remember the order users were added" → use Map, not Object.

terms.def: A statement that is true at the start of every iteration of a loop. The contract that proves the algorithm works.
terms.where: Binary search: "if the target exists, it is in [lo, hi]." Two-pointer: "all valid pairs lie between left and right."

terms.def: A tree where each node represents one character, and paths from root spell out words. Lookups by prefix are O(prefix length) regardless of dictionary size.
terms.where: Autocomplete, spellcheck, "does any word in this dictionary start with X?", IP routing tables.

terms.def: Every edge has equal cost (think 1 hop). Shortest path = fewest edges, found by BFS in one pass.
terms.where: BFS for shortest path. Word Ladder. Min steps to reach X. If a problem says "shortest path" and no weights are given, the answer is BFS — NOT DFS, NOT Dijkstra.

terms.def: Each edge has a numeric cost (time, distance, $). Shortest path = minimum TOTAL WEIGHT; BFS will not find it correctly. Use Dijkstra (non-negative weights) or Bellman-Ford (negatives allowed).
terms.where: Network routing. Cheapest flight with K stops. Dijkstra is the default; reach for Bellman-Ford only when an edge can be negative.

terms.def: Edges have a direction; `u → v` does NOT imply `v → u`. Models one-way streets, prerequisite chains, follower lists.
terms.where: Course Schedule (prereqs are directed). Topological sort REQUIRES directedness. Cycle detection on directed graphs needs the recursion-stack trick — plain visited is not enough.

terms.def: Edges are bidirectional; `u — v` means u and v are mutually neighbors. Models friendships, road adjacency, electrical connections.
terms.where: Number of Provinces. Friend circles. Number of Islands (grid as implicit undirected graph). Union-Find's natural domain.

terms.def: Directed graph with no cycles. Always has at least one source (in-degree 0) and one sink (out-degree 0). Every DAG has at least one valid topological order.
terms.where: Build systems. Course schedule. Spreadsheet recalc. If a topological sort succeeds, the input was a DAG; if it fails (cycle detected), it wasn't.

terms.def: Maximal subset of nodes mutually reachable. An undirected graph with N nodes and 0 edges has N components. Each DFS/BFS launched from an unvisited node sinks one whole component.
terms.where: Number of Islands. Number of Provinces. Friend circles. Universal pattern: outer loop over nodes; if unvisited → count++ and flood-fill.

terms.def: Does the graph contain a cycle? UNDIRECTED: DFS — a back-edge to an already-visited NON-PARENT node = cycle (or Union-Find). DIRECTED: DFS with a recursion-stack set (visited-in-current-path); a back-edge to an in-stack node = cycle.
terms.where: Course Schedule (can you finish? = is the prereq graph a DAG?). Deadlock detection. Detecting circular imports.

terms.def: Explore neighbors level by level. Uses a queue. First time you reach a node = shortest path (in edges).
terms.where: Shortest path in unweighted graph. Level-order tree traversal. Spreading infection / fire / water.

terms.def: Explore as deep as possible before backtracking. Uses recursion or an explicit stack.
terms.where: Counting connected components. Reachability. Tree traversals (in/pre/post). Cycle detection. Topological sort.

terms.def: Tree DFS traversal orderings. Pre-order: node → left → right. In-order: left → node → right (yields sorted output on a BST). Post-order: left → right → node (used when children's results feed the parent — e.g. tree height).
terms.where: BST → in-order gives sorted. Tree height → post-order. Serializing → pre-order.

terms.def: Linear ordering of a DAG (directed acyclic graph) such that every edge u → v has u before v. Detects cycles as a side effect.
terms.where: Course schedule. Build dependency resolution. Spreadsheet recalc order.

terms.def: Shortest path on a weighted graph with non-negative weights. BFS + priority queue.
terms.where: Maps/routing. Network latency. NOT needed for unweighted graphs (BFS is enough there).

terms.def: A structure for "are these two things in the same group?" with union(a,b) and find(a) operations. Near-O(1) amortized.
terms.where: Number of connected components. Detecting cycle in undirected graph. Kruskal's MST.

terms.def: Break a problem into overlapping subproblems, store each result so you do not recompute. Either top-down (memoized recursion) or bottom-up (fill a table).
terms.where: Coin change, edit distance, longest common subsequence, knapsack.

terms.def: A contiguous chunk of a string. "abc" has substrings "", "a", "ab", "abc", "b", "bc", "c".
terms.where: Longest substring without repeating chars (sliding window).

terms.def: An ordered selection of characters, NOT necessarily contiguous. "ace" is a subsequence of "abcde".
terms.where: Longest common subsequence (DP). Longest increasing subsequence.

terms.def: An array where prefix[i] = arr[0] + ... + arr[i]. Lets you compute the sum of any range in O(1).
terms.where: Range-sum queries. Sliding window over arrays that may contain negatives.

terms.def: A queue you can push/pop from BOTH ends in O(1). In JS, fake one with an array + index pointers.
terms.where: Rate limiter (evict front, push back). Sliding window maximum (monotonic deque).

terms.def: Big-O cost of an algorithm. TIME: how many operations as input N grows. SPACE: max additional memory the algorithm might hold at once. The input itself doesn't count — only auxiliary storage you allocate.
terms.where: Every interview problem ends with "what's the complexity?" Always state BOTH. Recursion counts toward space (call stack depth).
